studies.title: He Frowned And Turned Away
studies.meaning: The surah opens by reporting a frown in the third person, so the fault is stated before anyone is addressed. Only in the third ayah does the grammar turn to you, and the correction arrives as a question rather than a charge: how do you know. Two possibilities are then raised on the blind man's behalf, that he might be cleansed or that a reminder might do him good, and neither is asserted. Against that stands the one who thought himself in need of nothing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and one of the few passages with a well-attested occasion. The classical sources report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was occupied with leading men of Mecca whose acceptance would have mattered enormously to a small and pressured community, when a blind man came asking to be taught, and was not attended to. The surah was given about that moment. The reports name the man as Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum.

keyTerms.note: A verb for the face tightening in displeasure, distinct from anger. The Quran uses it in only one other place, of a man hardening his expression while deciding to reject a revelation he had just heard.
A reflexive form joining cleanness and growth, so the possibility raised for the blind man is an increase in him rather than a service done to him. The same verb returns twice in the following lines.
A form that means to seek or claim independence, built on the word for wealth. It names an attitude rather than a possession, which is why it can be applied to someone who is merely comfortable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on standing. A man's hearing depended on his lineage, his wealth and how many armed relatives he could call, and a blind man without means sat at the bottom of every one of those measures. Access to an assembly, a share in a caravan, protection on the road: all of it followed from rank. Someone with nothing to trade was, by the city's own arithmetic, not worth an hour.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for frowning occurs twice in the whole Quran. The other place describes a man in Mecca hardening his face as he turns from a revelation he has heard and cannot answer. The same physical gesture is reported of a rejecter there and corrected in the bearer of the message here, and the surah takes its name from the word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A revelation preserved for recitation contains a correction of the one who received it, which says something about the text before it says anything about the incident. Nothing is edited out. The correction is also framed as a question about knowledge rather than a rebuke about kindness: the objection is not that the man was treated coldly but that his prospects were unknown and were assumed anyway.

crossReferences.why: Contains the only other frown in the Quran, on a man deciding to dismiss what he has just heard.
Instructs the Prophet to stay with those who call on their Lord and not to look past them for finer company.
Forbids driving away those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking nothing but His face.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you gave someone a shorter answer than you would have given a person who mattered more to you. It is a small thing and it happens constantly. Pick one such person this week and give them the longer answer instead. You do not have to explain why, and they will not know anything happened.

studies.title: You Are Not Answerable
studies.meaning: The two men are set out in matching halves and the balance is exact. To the one who wants nothing, attention is given; from the one who came at speed and in awe, attention is withheld. Between them sits a line that removes the whole justification: you are not answerable for whether he purifies himself. The effort that looked like duty is quietly reclassified. What the passage corrects is not coldness toward the poor man but a calculation about the useful one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the same well-attested occasion as the opening lines. The community was small, harassed and short of protection, and the acceptance of a few leading men would have changed its position in the city overnight. The commentators are clear that the concern behind the frown was the message rather than the messenger's comfort, which is what makes the correction here so pointed.

keyTerms.gloss: you attend to, you face toward
keyTerms.note: To turn yourself toward someone and make yourself available. The form suggests effort maintained rather than a single glance, so the contrast is between sustained attention and the lapse described four words later.

A verb for moving with purpose, used of running an errand and of striving after something. It puts the blind man in motion while the other party is stationary, which is the passage's quiet arithmetic.
From a root about amusement and diversion. It occurs once more in the Quran, of men whom trade and selling do not divert from remembering God, so the word carries no sense of legitimate busyness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A blind man in seventh-century Arabia moved through the city by memory and by the arm of whoever would lend one. Reaching a particular person meant asking directions, waiting where he was told, and arriving late. The word describing him as hurrying is doing real work: he had covered ground that cost him more than it cost anyone else in the room, in order to ask a question.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for being diverted here appears in only one other place in the Quran, in a description of men whom neither trade nor selling distracts from the remembrance of God. Set beside that, the choice of word is severe: the same term that praises those who are not diverted by business is applied to a moment of attention given to business.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The line in the middle removes results from the account. Whether the wealthy man is cleansed is explicitly not the messenger's responsibility, which means the strategy that produced the frown was built on a duty that did not exist. Guidance is not a yield to be maximised. That reframing protects everyone who has ever tried to be useful to God by ranking people, and it is stated as a matter of fact rather than as a reproach.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for being diverted, there of men whom trade does not divert from remembering God.
Tells the Prophet he is a reminder only and not in control over them, the same removal of responsibility for results.
Asks whether the Prophet would compel people to believe, after saying that God could have made everyone believe.

studies.applyIt: Notice, once today, who you are steering a conversation toward and who you are steering it away from. Most people find the sorting is not conscious and is not about liking. It is about who seems worth the time. You are not being asked to change the room. Just watch yourself do the arithmetic, and see whether it survives being watched.

studies.title: Pages In Honoured Hands
studies.meaning: A single word of refusal closes the incident, and the subject changes to what was being withheld. It is called a reminder, and access to it is put in the most open terms available: whoever wills remembers it. Then the surah describes where it is kept rather than what it says. Pages held in honour, raised up, kept pure, in the hands of those who write. Nothing is said about content, only about custody, and the description keeps rising away from the room the surah began in.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The lines follow directly on a correction about who was given attention, and the commentators read the sequence as deliberate: after a scene about rank, the message itself is described as available to anyone who wants it. No occasion is reported for these particular ayat. Written scripture was familiar in Arabia through the Jewish and Christian communities of the peninsula, though Mecca itself had little of it.

keyTerms.note: Loose written leaves rather than a bound volume, which is what a book was in that world. The same word names the scriptures given to earlier prophets and, elsewhere, the records spread open on the last day.
A passive participle, so the purity is something done to the pages rather than a quality they have. It belongs to the same root as the words for cleansing a person and for the ritual state of purity.
Read by the commentators as those who write out a text and also, from the same root, as those who carry a message between parties. Both senses describe an intermediary who adds nothing of his own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing in Mecca was a specialist trade. Materials were scarce, scribes were hired for contracts and letters, and the physical care of a document mattered: sheets were wrapped, kept off the ground, and handled by named people who could be held responsible for them. A description of pages that are honoured, raised and kept clean would have read as a description of custody procedure, not as praise.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for those who write shares its three root letters with a word four lines from the end of the same surah, where faces on the last day are described as shining. The surah rhymes on that sound in both places. What links them in the lexicon is the idea of something being uncovered or made plain, which is what a scribe does to speech.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing a text by its custody rather than its content makes a claim about transmission. The pages are honoured, elevated and purified, and the hands are noble, so nothing in the chain is described as adding or subtracting. Set immediately after a scene in which a human being sorted his listeners by rank, the passage locates the message in a place where no such sorting has occurred, and then offers it to whoever wills.

crossReferences.why: Also describes purified pages, and says what is in them: writings that stand upright.
Places the recitation in a hidden book that only the purified touch, a close parallel in vocabulary.
Ends another surah by locating the Quran in a preserved tablet, the same move from message to keeping.

studies.applyIt: Handle a copy of the Quran today the way this passage describes its pages: off the floor, clean hands, put back rather than left open face down. The point is not the object. It is that a minute of physical care changes the attention you bring to the next thing you read in it, which is easier to test than to argue about.

studies.title: How Ungrateful He Is
studies.meaning: An exclamation of dismissal is followed immediately by a question that answers it. What is the human being made from. The reply is deliberately unflattering: a drop, and from that a proportioning, and then a way made easy. Three stages, each in two or three words, and none of them anything he arranged. Scholars read the eased way as either the passage of birth or the road of guidance and choice, and the sources keep both. Either way the ingratitude is measured against the smallness of the beginning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage turns from the incident that opened the surah to the human being in general, which the commentators treat as the surah's method: a particular failure of attention is widened into the species. No occasion is reported for these lines. The audience were people who traced descent carefully and took pride in it, and being asked what they were actually made of cut against the whole system of lineage.

keyTerms.note: An exclamatory construction, rare in the Quran. The root joins covering something over with denying it, so ingratitude and disbelief are one word here: what is covered is a benefit received.
The word for the small amount of water left in a skin or a bucket. Applied to human origin it names the beginning by its quantity, which is the point being made against a man's estimate of himself.
To measure, apportion and determine. The verb covers both giving a thing its physical measure and setting what will happen to it, and Arabic does not separate the two senses here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Measuring was constant work. Grain was apportioned by known volumes, water was drawn in fixed skins, cloth was cut to a measure, and a caravan's load was calculated to the animal. The verb used here for proportioning a human being was the same one used for those daily calculations. Hearing your own body described with the word for weighing out a ration placed you inside somebody else's arithmetic.
studies.didYouKnow: The exclamation that opens this passage uses a form Arabic reserves for astonishment, and the same construction is used in the surah placed six chapters earlier of a man calculating how to dismiss a revelation. Both passages pair it with the verb for perishing. This surah then answers its own exclamation with a question about material, which is unusual: the rebuke is settled by embryology rather than by argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ingratitude is presented as a failure of memory about origins rather than as a moral coldness. The Arabic makes disbelief and thanklessness the same word, so refusing God and forgetting what you were made from are not two problems. And the eased way, whichever reading is taken, is listed among the things done for him, which means even the capacity to choose appears on the side of what was given.

crossReferences.why: Traces the same sequence from a drop to hearing and sight, and then to a way shown, either grateful or ungrateful.
Notes the same distance, made from a drop and then openly disputing, in a single line.
Puts the contrast most sharply, a man from a drop who becomes an open adversary.

studies.applyIt: Say out loud, once, the plainest true sentence about how you started: a drop of fluid, no say in any of it. It sounds crude because it is meant to. Then get on with your day. The passage does not ask you to feel small for long. It asks you to hold the fact for as long as it takes to say it.

studies.title: Then He Gave Him A Grave
studies.meaning: Two more stages complete the sequence, and both are done to the human being rather than by him. He is made to die and then given a grave, and the second verb is causative: not that God buried him, but that God made burial his portion. The raising is left to a condition, when He wills. Then the summary arrives, and it is a verdict rather than a threat. He has not discharged what was required of him. And with that the surah sends him to look at his dinner.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage completes an argument that began by asking what the human being is made from, and the commentators read the whole run from origin to grave to resurrection as one sentence about a life that was arranged at every point. No occasion is reported. The abrupt turn to food at the end reflects an audience whose objection to the resurrection was practical rather than philosophical.

keyTerms.note: A causative from the word for a grave, occurring once in the Quran. The commentators note it does not say God buried him but that He assigned him burial, treating the covering of the dead as a dignity granted rather than a fact of decay.
From a root about spreading a thing out after it has been folded away, used of unrolling a scroll. Resurrection is pictured as something opened out again rather than as something built a second time.
The verb covers completing, settling and paying off, the word used of clearing a debt. The negative particle carries a sense of not yet, which leaves the account open rather than closed against him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in Arabia was quick and shallow, done before nightfall in ground that was often more stone than soil, and it mattered greatly. A body left uncovered was a disgrace to a whole family and an invitation to animals, and one of the recognised injuries a tribe could inflict was to prevent a burial. A grave was therefore not a natural end but something a community provided, at cost, for its own.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb saying that a grave was given occurs once in the whole Quran, and its form is the one Arabic uses for causing something rather than doing it. Classical grammarians drew the point out: the sentence credits the custom of covering the dead to God rather than to human beings, so a practice every community assumes is listed here among the things done for a person who did not ask.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Every verb in the sequence has God as its subject and the human being as its object, including the ones about dying and being buried, which people normally think of as things that simply happen. The one clause with a human subject is the failure. That distribution is the passage's argument: the whole arc was arranged, and the single unarranged thing in it, the discharge of what was asked, is the thing left undone.

crossReferences.why: Shows the first burial being taught by a bird, so covering the dead arrives as instruction rather than instinct.
Gives the same three stages in one line: from the earth, returned to it, and brought out again.
Sets out the identical order, gave you life, then causes death, then gives life again, and names the response.

studies.applyIt: Walk through a graveyard this week, or if there is none nearby, stop at one on a map and read the dates. The passage treats the grave as something provided rather than something suffered. Ten minutes among the provided graves of strangers does more with that idea than any amount of thinking about it will.

studies.title: Then We Split The Ground
studies.meaning: The instruction to look at food is answered with a process rather than a menu. Water is poured, and the verb is doubled in the Arabic for emphasis; the ground is split open, and that verb is doubled too. Only then does anything grow, and the list moves from the staple outward: grain, then vines, then green fodder, then olives and palms, then gardens too thick to see through. Nothing here is a miracle. The point is that the reader has never once watched it happen.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage is the surah's answer to a demand for evidence about the resurrection, and the commentators note that the argument is deliberately domestic: not the sky or the mountains but the plate in front of the listener. No occasion is reported. Grain, dates, olives and vines were the four things a Meccan household bought, grew or imported, so the list is the local diet in order of importance.

keyTerms.note: A word from the vocabulary of thick necks and heavy shoulders, used of men and of camels long before it is used of trees. Applied to gardens it makes them crowded and strong rather than merely green.

The same doubling used again, on a verb for tearing something open along a line. Soil is described as opened by force from above rather than as softening, which is what a shoot pushing through actually does.
From a verb meaning to cut, so the word names a plant by the fact that it is harvested green and grows back. It occurs once in the Quran, and it belongs to animals rather than to people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The valley of Mecca grew almost nothing. Grain came up the road from Yemen or down from Syria, dates and vines came from the oases, and a household's food was assembled from other people's ground. So a list of crops was a list of places, seasons and the men who moved them. Being told to look at your food was being told to look at a supply line several weeks long that you had never seen the start of.
studies.didYouKnow: The first two verbs in this passage each repeat themselves in the form Arabic uses for emphasis, pouring a pouring and splitting a splitting, and then the construction is dropped for the rest of the list. Only the two actions nobody sees are intensified. The growth that follows, which people do watch, is given in plain nouns with no emphasis at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question about the last day by describing lunch. What it establishes is that the process the listener depends on daily is already the process he says is impossible: something is put into the ground, the ground is broken open, and what comes out is alive. Nothing is claimed beyond that. The argument works by refusing to be impressive, which is why it is put in the imperative, look.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same sequence, water then gardens and grain, and names it likewise as the resurrection.
Calls the dead land a sign, lists the same crops, and points out that human hands did not make them.
Traces the same order from water to the shoot to grain, dates, vines and olives, in one long ayah.

studies.applyIt: Take the single item on your plate today that came out of the ground and hold it for a moment before eating it. A grain of rice, an olive, a date. You did not watch any part of what made it, and you could not have done any part of it. Eat it slowly enough that the fact registers. That is the whole of what this passage asks.

studies.title: The Day A Man Runs
studies.meaning: The list of what grows closes with fruit and one word whose meaning the earliest scholars would not fix, and then sums the whole harvest up as something to use, for you and for your animals. One line later the deafening arrives and the subject is people rather than plants. The first thing said about that day is not fire or a book. It is that a man runs from his brother, and then from his mother and his father, and the running is away from exactly the people a life is built out of.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah moves in one line from the food supply to the last day, and the commentators treat the abruptness as the design: the same ground that feeds a family is where the family comes apart. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Kinship in Arabia was not sentiment but structure, the mechanism by which a person was fed, defended, married and avenged, which is what makes the flight described here so severe.

keyTerms.note: A word the classical scholars glossed as pasture or as what animals eat, while declining to be more precise. It occurs once in the Quran and is the most discussed single word in this surah.
From a verb about a sound so loud it stuns the ear. The day is named by what it does to hearing, and the word occurs once in the Quran, so it names nothing else.
Used of an animal breaking away and of a man running from a battle line. It is not the word for leaving or withdrawing; it describes flight that is unplanned and undignified.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A person alone in Arabia was a person who could be killed without consequence. Kin were your food in a bad year, your defence on the road, your standing in an assembly and the reason anyone would avenge you. Brothers held property together, a mother's people were the fallback when a father's failed. Running from all of that at once described not grief but the removal of every structure a listener had.
studies.didYouKnow: One of the earliest authorities is reported to have recited the word for herbage in this passage, asked aloud what it meant, and then stopped himself, saying that pressing further into it was affectation. The remark became famous as a model of restraint in interpretation, and the word remains the one place in the surah where the classical commentaries record a deliberate refusal to decide.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures the day by what it dissolves rather than by what it inflicts. Nothing has been said yet about punishment; what has been said is that the strongest bonds a human being has stop functioning. That establishes accountability as individual in a way no argument could, because it removes the intermediaries rather than arguing against them, and it does so with the family named one by one.

crossReferences.why: Says no parent will avail his child and no child his parent, in the same territory of failed kinship.
Has a man wanting to ransom himself with his sons, his wife, his brother and everyone on earth.
States that when the trumpet is blown no ties of kinship remain between them, and no questions are asked.

studies.applyIt: Call the relative you have been meaning to call. Not because of the fear in this passage, but because the passage names the exact set of people you will one day not be able to reach and lists them in order. One of them is a phone call away today. That is the only part of the ayah you can act on.

studies.title: Enough To Occupy Him
studies.meaning: The list of relatives finishes with the two that classical readers say a person clings to hardest, a spouse and children, so the order has been running toward greater attachment all along. Then the reason is given in one line, and it is not that the ties have been forbidden. Each person simply has a matter of his own that is enough for him. After that the surah stops describing the day and starts describing faces, and it gives the bright ones three words while it is still gathering itself to describe the others.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The closing movement of the surah answers its opening scene: it began with a face turning away from a man of no standing, and it ends by sorting all faces into two kinds without a word about rank. The commentators note the symmetry. No occasion is reported for these lines. The final sorting uses no category the audience in Mecca could have inherited or bought.

keyTerms.note: The feminine of the word for a companion, used rather than the ordinary term for a wife. It names her by the fact of accompanying him, which makes the flight described in the same line sharper.

A person's own affair or state of business. It is a plain, almost administrative word, and using it for the crisis of the last day is deliberate understatement: everyone is simply busy with their own case.
From a root about removing a covering, which also gives the word for dawn breaking. A bright face is described as an unveiled one, so the light is what was there once the covering came off.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a raid or a flight from a burning camp, everyone knew what happened: people ran, and the running was individual no matter how loyal the household had been the day before. Poets recorded such moments and were not gentle about them. The surah's phrase, a matter that is enough for him, describes something the audience had seen on human faces, and it needed no theology to be understood.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes faces on that day as laughing in only this place. The word is used once in the whole Book. The bright faces here are given three descriptions in two short lines, shining, laughing and glad, while the other kind get a covering of dust and then something darker, so the two panels are unequal in length as well as in content.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason given for the collapse of family is administrative rather than moral: each person has enough of his own to attend to. That makes accountability a matter of capacity rather than of punishment, and it is far more unsettling than a prohibition would have been. The sorting that follows is done on faces, the most public thing about a person and the one thing nobody arranges, which is where the surah began.

crossReferences.why: Also sorts the day by faces, some radiant and looking at their Lord, others expecting a crushing blow.
Divides the same day into humbled faces and faces at ease, using the identical two-panel structure.
Describes a day when some faces turn bright and some turn dark, and stakes the outcome on that alone.

studies.applyIt: Look at your own face in the mirror tonight for a few seconds longer than you need to. You do not choose what it does when it is at rest, and other people read it all day without telling you. The passage ends by sorting people on exactly that, the part of you that is public and unarranged. Notice it once, without fixing it.

studies.title: Dust, And Then Darkness
studies.meaning: Two lines close the surah, and the first is a physical description rather than a judgement. Something dark settles over the faces already covered in dust, so the covering happens twice and the second layer is worse than the first. Only in the final line are the people named, and they are named twice over, as those who covered the truth and those who broke through every restraint. The naming comes last, after the reader has already seen what the faces look like.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah closes on the same theme it opened with, a face and what is written on it, having travelled from a frown in a Meccan room to the sorting of every face at the end. No occasion is reported for the closing ayat. The commentators note that the two nouns used here name a settled condition rather than an act, which fits a surah whose subject throughout has been dispositions rather than incidents.

keyTerms.note: A verb for something coming over a person and pressing down, used elsewhere of humiliation settling on faces. It describes an arrival from outside rather than a change in the face itself.

Related to words for smoke and for a mean or stinting hand. It occurs once in the Quran, and the commentators describe it as a blackness laid over the dust already there, a second covering rather than a deeper one.
From a root about splitting open, which also gives the word for daybreak. Here it names people who have broken through a boundary, so the image is of a limit torn rather than a rule ignored.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dust on a face was the mark of a man who had lost. It settled on anyone thrown down in a fight, on prisoners walked back from a raid, on the poor who slept where they worked. Adding soot to it doubled the image, since soot belonged to cooking fires and to the lowest work in a household. Both were things a Meccan of standing spent money and effort never to be seen wearing.
studies.didYouKnow: The two nouns that end this surah share their plural pattern with the two that describe the scribes near its beginning, and all four occur at the rhyme. The pattern is used at the top of the surah for those who are noble and dutiful, and at the bottom for those who deny and transgress. Both closing words appear nowhere else in the Quran in this form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah ends by describing a condition rather than announcing a sentence. Nothing is said about what happens to these people; what is given is what they look like, and the naming follows the appearance rather than causing it. That order matters. It presents the final state as something that becomes visible rather than something imposed, which is consistent with a chapter that has treated faces as evidence from its first word.

crossReferences.why: Contrasts faces with no dust or humiliation on them against faces overtaken by exactly that.
Uses the same verb for humiliation settling over people whose eyes are lowered on that day.
Describes the opposite face, where the brightness of ease can be recognised on it.

studies.applyIt: The surah began with a face turning away and ends with faces being read. Choose one person today and give them your face while they talk, phone down, eyes up, for the whole of what they say. It takes two minutes and it is the exact thing the first ayah of this surah is about.
